Name: superseded_theory_representations
Title: Do Scientific Foundation Models Encode Superseded Theories Alongside Correct Ones? Probing for Historical-Scientific Fault Lines
Short Hypothesis: Scientific foundation models are trained on corpora spanning decades of literature that contain both currently accepted mechanisms and superseded/refuted theories (e.g., Lamarckian inheritance, phlogiston-style heat reasoning, incorrect reaction mechanisms, discredited protein-folding heuristics). We hypothesize that models internally encode BOTH the correct and superseded versions of a mechanism as distinguishable, linearly separable directions, that the model's *default* output can be tipped toward the superseded theory by simple contextual or activation-level nudges, and that the relative representational strength of correct-vs-superseded directions predicts where the model will emit scientifically outdated reasoning. This is a measurable, previously unstudied failure mode distinct from generic hallucination.
Related Work: Existing interpretability work on scientific foundation models (BERTology-Meets-Biology, SAEs for protein features, universally-converging-matter representations) probes whether *currently correct* concepts are encoded, and mechanism-fidelity/causal-probing work (including our own prior proposals) tests whether correct laws are causally used. None ask whether *incorrect, historically superseded* scientific theories co-reside in representation space and compete with correct ones. Work on temporal/outdated knowledge in LLMs focuses on factual staleness (dates, entities, current events), not on scientific *mechanistic* theories that were once accepted and later refuted. Hallucination-detection literature treats errors as unstructured noise; we instead hypothesize a *structured* error source: coherent legacy theories embedded in the training distribution. Our proposal is novel in framing model errors as historical-theory competition, providing paired correct/superseded concept probes and a 'theory-competition' diagnostic tied to conceptual history rather than recency.
Abstract: Scientific foundation models learn from decades of literature that mixes today's accepted mechanisms with theories that were once believed and later refuted. We ask a simple but unexplored question: do these models internally represent superseded scientific theories, and can those legacy representations override correct ones? Unlike generic hallucination, we hypothesize a structured failure mode in which a coherent, historically-held-but-wrong mechanism co-resides with the correct mechanism as a distinct, linearly separable representational direction, and competes to shape outputs. We curate ~10 paired (correct-theory, superseded-theory) mechanisms across chemistry, biology, physics, and medicine (e.g., valence-shell vs. phlogiston-style reasoning about combustion/oxidation, Mendelian/molecular vs. Lamarckian inheritance framings, correct vs. classic textbook-wrong SN1/SN2 mechanistic attributions, heat-as-caloric vs. kinetic descriptions). For each, we (1) build minimal contrastive text pairs and fit linear probes to locate correct and superseded directions in open scientific/text models, (2) measure their representational strength and separability across layers, (3) test whether small contextual priming or activation steering along the superseded direction flips the model's stated mechanism, and (4) test whether the correct-vs-superseded probe-strength ratio predicts the model's default answer and its error rate on held-out mechanistic questions. We validate on multiple open models (scientific LLMs and general LLMs), comparing against a random-direction null and a modern-only control concept. The result is a reproducible diagnostic of when and why scientific models regress to outdated theories, informing safe deployment and dataset curation.
Experiments: 1. Mechanism curation: Assemble ~10 paired mechanisms, each with (a) the currently accepted description, (b) a historically-accepted-but-superseded description, and (c) a set of mechanistic probe questions with a scientifically-correct answer key. Domains and examples: chemistry (combustion/oxidation via oxygen electron transfer vs. phlogiston release; caloric vs. kinetic theory of heat; common textbook-wrong vs. correct SN1/SN2 and Markovnikov attributions); biology/medicine (molecular/Mendelian vs. Lamarckian acquired-inheritance framing; germ theory vs. miasma disease causation; correct vs. discredited 'junk DNA is functionless' framing); physics (special-relativity vs. luminiferous-aether propagation; correct vs. Aristotelian force-motion). 2. Contrastive stimulus construction: For each pair, generate minimal contrastive sentence sets that differ only in the mechanistic claim, holding topic/vocabulary matched. 3. Probe localization: For each layer of each open model (e.g., a scientific LLM such as a Galactica-style or SciBERT-family model, plus general open LLMs like Llama/Mistral/Pythia), extract representations of the mechanistic token spans and fit linear probes to distinguish correct vs. superseded framings; record per-layer separability (accuracy), direction geometry (cosine between correct/superseded directions), and representational strength (probe margin). 4. Default-output measurement: Query each model with neutral mechanistic questions; score whether the default answer is correct or superseded using the answer key (auto-graded with a rubric + manual spot-check). 5. Steering test: Add alpha*(superseded_direction) at the localized layer, sweep alpha, and measure the rate at which correct default answers flip to superseded answers; compare to random-direction and modern-only-concept (no superseded counterpart) controls to establish specificity. 6. Priming test: Prepend brief in-context passages written in the superseded framing (matched-length correct-framing prime as control) and measure output flip rate; compare with the activation-steering results. 7. Predictive analysis: Test whether the correct-vs-superseded probe-strength ratio (per mechanism, per model) predicts (i) the default answer and (ii) the error rate under mild adversarial priming, via correlation/AUROC across mechanisms and models. 8. Scaling/training analysis: Compare across model sizes and, where available, scientific-corpus vs. general-corpus models to test whether legacy-theory strength depends on training data composition. Metrics: probe separability, correct/superseded direction cosine, default-answer correctness, steering/priming flip rate vs. controls, and predictive AUROC of the strength-ratio for outdated-answer emission. Deliverable: an open paired-theory benchmark and a per-model 'legacy-theory susceptibility' score.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Some superseded theories may be so rare in training data that no direction exists (null result); this is itself informative and we report which theories are/aren't encoded. 2. Grading whether an answer is 'superseded' vs. merely 'wrong/hallucinated' requires careful rubrics; we mitigate with explicit answer keys, matched controls, and manual spot-checks to separate structured legacy errors from unstructured noise. 3. Linear probes may miss nonlinearly encoded theories; we add nonlinear-probe robustness checks and treat linear results as a lower bound. 4. Activation steering can push off-manifold and cause artifacts; we cross-validate with the purely input-level priming test, so conclusions do not rely solely on edits. 5. Availability of strong open scientific LLMs is limited; we scope to available public models and include general LLMs, framing cross-model comparison as part of the finding. 6. Curating clean correct/superseded pairs is nontrivial and requires domain vetting; we restrict to well-documented historical theory shifts to ensure ground-truth clarity.
